papers.title_in_file: Quantum ensemble learning with a programmable superconducting processor
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, framework and setup, MNIST QNN results, QCNN results, conclusion; methods and supplement not read
papers.what_it_is: An experimental paper that adapts AdaBoost to quantum classifiers (Adaboost.Q) and runs it on a superconducting processor.

assertions.value: The authors report that Adaboost.Q raised the testing accuracy of a ten-qubit QNN classifier on the full MNIST test set from 80.5% to 86.7%, measured on a superconducting processor.
quotes: A notable increase of the accuracy is observed, from 80.5% to 86.7% over the first two iterations, after which the accuracy saturates.
We experimentally demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a fully programmable superconducting quantum processor
assertions.certainty_reason: One experiment on one device and one task.

assertions.value: The authors report that an ensemble of two base QCNN classifiers reached 100% testing accuracy on a three-class phase classification task, while a single QCNN classifier was limited to around 80%.
quotes: For a single QCNN classifier, we find that the testing accuracy for the three-class classification task is limited to around 80%.
Finally, by combining only two base classifiers, the ensemble classifier achieves a testing accuracy of 100% on the whole test set
assertions.certainty_reason: One experiment on one task with variational-circuit-prepared test states.
assertions.reader_inference: The test states are approximate ground states prepared by variational circuits, so the task is a quantum-data demonstration, not a classical-data benchmark.

assertions.value: The authors state that the classifiers ran on a fully programmable superconducting quantum processor, with a 15-qubit QCNN used for the quantum-data task.
quotes: on a fully programmable superconducting quantum processor [12].
For the quantum data classification task, we build a QCNN classifier with a carefully designed one-dimensional (1D) chain consisting of 15 qubits.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its experimental setup, p.3.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Machine Learning for UAV Swarm Intrusion Detection
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, QML model descriptions (skimmed), QML benchmark discussion, conclusion; individual result tables read only as extracted numbers
papers.what_it_is: A simulation benchmark of quantum kernels, variational QNNs and quantum-trained neural networks against classical baselines for UAV swarm intrusion detection.

assertions.value: The authors report that the eight-layer Hybrid QNN, with eight qubits, reached an accuracy of 0.948 and an F1-score of 0.967, the best performance in their benchmark.
quotes: The best performance is achieved by the eight-layer Hybrid QNN, which requires only eight qubits, 18 classical, and 64 quantum trainable parameters to reach an accuracy of 0.948, F1-score of 0.967, sensitivity of 0.972, and specificity of 0.838.
assertions.certainty_reason: One benchmark on one simulated dataset.
assertions.reader_inference: The dataset is simulated, so the figures say nothing about real network traffic.

assertions.value: The authors report that deeper variational QNNs showed sensitivity approaching 0.99 with specificity falling as low as 0.04, and accuracy about ten percentage points below classical models.
quotes: as circuit depth increases, sensitivity approaches 0.99 while specificity collapses to as low as 0.04
resulting in overall accuracies approximately ten percentage points lower than classical models
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one benchmark; the barren-plateau explanation is the authors' attribution.

assertions.value: The authors state that the benchmark uses a 120 k-flow simulation corpus with five attack types, and that real hardware runs are left to future work.
quotes: Leveraging a 120 k-flow simulation corpus that covers five attack types
Future work will extend the benchmark to federated and adversarially robust settings, incorporate real hardware runs
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its data and scope, Abstract and Conclusion.
assertions.reader_inference: The text implies the quantum models were simulated, not run on devices, because hardware runs are listed as future work.

papers.title_in_file: Hybrid Quantum Neural Networks with Amplitude Encoding for Credit Recovery Rate Prediction
papers.version_note: File is arXiv v6 dated 25 Jan 2026.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, XGBoost comparison and discussion, section 5.5, conclusion, limitations, future work, Appendix B; data and methodology sections skimmed
papers.what_it_is: A hybrid amplitude-encoded quantum neural network for credit recovery-rate regression, compared with classical networks, angle-encoded QML and XGBoost on simulators.

assertions.value: The authors report an RMSE of 0.228 for the amplitude-encoded hybrid model, against 0.246 for classical neural networks and 0.242 for QML with angle encoding, on 1,725 observations with 256 features.
quotes: achieving a lower Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) of 0.228, compared to 0.246 and 0.242, respectively.
on a global recovery rate dataset comprising 1,725 observations and 256 features from 1996 to 2023.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one dataset in simulation.
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract does not say which figure belongs to which baseline beyond the order of the sentence.

assertions.value: The authors state that the amplitude-encoded model does not clearly beat XGBoost: it has a higher average RMSE in cross-validation and outperforms XGBoost in leave-one-out cross-validation.
quotes: When compared to XGBoost, the proposed QML model with Amplitude Encoding does not demonstrate clearly superior performance.
Moreover, in the leave-one-out cross-validation, the proposed QML model outperforms XGBoost.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one dataset in simulation.

assertions.value: The authors state that all QML models in the paper were developed and tested on quantum simulators rather than real quantum hardware, and that the study should be read as a proof of concept.
quotes: First, all QML models in this paper are developed and tested using quantum simulators rather than real quantum hardware.
the present study should be interpreted as a proof of concept demonstrating methodological feasibility rather than a cost-efficient alternative to classical machine-learning systems.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own stated limitation, Section 6.1.
assertions.reader_inference: Appendix B reports a preliminary run of only the angle-encoded model on a Rigetti QPU, so the statement holds for the main results, not for that appendix.

papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, results 2.1 to 2.4 (text, not every table), conclusion, methods software and hardware paragraph; supplementary derivations not read
papers.what_it_is: A hybrid photonic-classical knowledge-distillation method in which shot-limited photonic features condition a compressed student network.

assertions.value: The authors state that across MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10, PQKD traces a controllable compression-accuracy frontier and remains close to teacher performance on simpler benchmarks under aggressive convolutional compression.
quotes: Across MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10, PQKD traces a controllable compression
remaining close to teacher performance on simpler benchmarks under aggressive convolutional compression.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result on three public image benchmarks, mean over five runs.

assertions.value: The authors report that on CIFAR-10 the teacher network remained stronger than the PQKD student in both training and validation accuracy under partial convolutional compression.
quotes: For CIFAR-10, the teacher remains stronger in both training and validation accuracy, reflecting increased task complexity under the same compression budget.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one benchmark.

assertions.value: The authors report that performance degrades predictably with finite sampling, consistent with shot-noise scaling.
quotes: Performance degrades predictably with finite sampling, consistent with shot-noise scaling
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result fitted to a shot-noise model, in simulation.

assertions.value: The authors state that photonic sampling was executed via the ORCA simulator backend in CUDA-Q, and that the same experiment can be run on ORCA Computing's ptseries backend when available.
quotes: was executed via the ORCA simulator backend in CUDA-Q
when available, the same experiment can be run against ORCA Computing's ptseries backend
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its experimental setup, Section 4.7.
assertions.reader_inference: The reported results come from a simulator, not from photonic hardware.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Adaptive Self-Attention for Quantum Transformer Models
papers.version_note: File is arXiv v4 dated 23 Jun 2026.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, experiment details, results 4.3, hardware validation 4.9, limitations 4.11, conclusion; ablations and appendices skimmed
papers.what_it_is: A hybrid Transformer with a 36-parameter quantum circuit replacing one value projection, tested against a capacity-matched classical bottleneck.

assertions.value: The authors report that a capacity-matched classical bottleneck with the same parameter budget matches the PQC on the error metrics, and they attribute the gain to the low-rank value-projection bottleneck, not to quantumness.
quotes: find that it matches the PQC on the error metrics.
The gain is therefore attributable to the low-rank value-projection bottleneck (an architectural parsimony principle), not to quantumness
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical control on synthetic benchmarks and one real dataset.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper itself finds no quantum-specific accuracy gain in this case study.

assertions.value: The authors state that, across nine synthetic benchmarks and the real-world ETTh1 dataset, QASA improves on a full-capacity classical Transformer for chaotic and trend-dominated signals.
quotes: Across nine synthetic benchmarks and the real-world ETTh1 dataset, QASA improves on a full-capacity classical Transformer for chaotic and trend-dominated signals.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result; the paper reports most paired t-tests as not significant.

assertions.value: The authors report that on an IBM processor, inference-only one-step MAE on the chaotic logistic task rose from 0.0093 to 0.0100 (7.5%) relative to noiseless simulation.
quotes: On chaotic logistic the one-step MAE rises only from 0.0093 to 0.0100 (7.5%)
inference-on-hardware validation of an already-trained model
assertions.certainty_reason: One device, two tasks, 16 test windows each, inference only.

assertions.value: The authors state that model training is performed on a classical state-vector simulator, that quantum baseline comparisons use n = 3 random seeds, and that most pairwise t-tests therefore do not reach significance.
quotes: Model training is performed on a classical state-vector simulator
Quantum baseline comparisons use n = 3 random seeds due to the high cost of quantum simulation
Most pairwise t-tests therefore do not reach
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own stated limitations, Section 4.11.

papers.title_in_file: Stochastic Quantum Spiking Neural Networks with Quantum Memory and Local Learning
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, experiments V (hardware, MNIST family, MNIST-DVS, N-ISAC text), conclusion; model derivations and appendices not read in full
papers.what_it_is: A multi-qubit stochastic quantum spiking neuron with internal quantum memory and a local learning rule, tested by simulation and on IBM hardware.

assertions.value: The authors report that the SQSNN model consistently achieved the highest test accuracy across the MNIST, FMNIST and KMNIST datasets, with the number of trainable parameters fixed across models.
assertions.anchor: Section V, comparative evaluation on MNIST, FMNIST, KMNIST
quotes: the SQSNN model consistently achieves the highest test accuracy across all three datasets
Experimental results compare different models by fixing the same number of trainable parameters across all models.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result on public image datasets, simulated.

assertions.value: The authors report that local training of the SQSNN on the USPS dataset on IBM ibm brisbane reached a peak test accuracy of nearly 95% without error mitigation (M = 1, Msyn = 5), and around 98% with error mitigation at M = 5 and Msyn = 5.
quotes: With M = 1 and Msyn = 5, the SQSNN model is seen to achieve a peak test accuracy of nearly 95%, even in the absence of QEM.
Using the same hardware, Fig. 7(b) plots the test accuracy obtained by the SQSNN model on the USPS dataset as a function of training iterations with QEM.
In particular, with M = 5 and Msyn = 5, SQSNN obtains a test accuracy around 98% at around 40 iterations
assertions.certainty_reason: One device, one small dataset.

assertions.value: The authors state that, because direct evaluation needs a large quantum processor, the benchmark results use classical simulations with a surrogate gradient-based approach to approximate the learning dynamics of the local rule.
quotes: its direct evaluation requires a quantum processor of sufficient scale to handle benchmarks of practical interest
we henceforth employ classical simulations using a surrogate gradient-based approach to approximate the learning dynamics of the proposed rule
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of how its benchmark results were produced, Section V.

papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, Theorem 1 statement, experimental setup and results text V, conclusion; appendix proof not read
papers.what_it_is: Two quantum imitation-learning algorithms, Q-BC and Q-GAIL, that use variational quantum circuits as policies, tested in simulation on control tasks.

assertions.value: The authors report that Q-BC and Q-GAIL mimic experts and achieve expert-level performance, and that no performance degradations are observed against the DNN-based BC and GAIL.
quotes: The proposed QIL algorithms, Q-BC and Q-GAIL, are able to successfully mimic experts from expert data and achieve expert-level performance.
no performance degradations are observed in the corresponding quantum versions, i.e., Q-BC and Q-GAIL.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result on a few small control tasks, simulated.

assertions.value: The authors state that they conducted the experiments with Tensorflow Quantum and Cirq to simulate quantum systems.
quotes: We conduct experiments with Tensorflow Quantum [86] and Cirq [87] to simulate quantum systems.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its experimental setup, Section V.C.
assertions.reader_inference: The results come from simulation, not from quantum hardware.

assertions.value: The paper states, under its Assumptions, an error bound for Q-BC that grows exponentially with the quantum measurement error and linearly with the square root of the optimization error.
quotes: can see that the error bound grows exponentially regarding the quantum measurement error and grows linearly with respect to the square root of the optimization error
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 1, Section IV, proof in the appendix (proof not read by this reader).

assertions.value: The authors state that QIL algorithms have the potential to be run on quantum computers and thus enjoy the quantum speed-up.
quotes: QIL algorithms have the potential to be run on quantum computers and thus enjoy the quantum speed-up
assertions.certainty_reason: An author expectation; no speed-up is measured.
assertions.reader_inference: The experiments are simulated, so no speed-up is demonstrated.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Annealing for Single Image Super-Resolution
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, background, evaluation setup, results text, runtime discussion, conclusion; algorithm derivations skimmed
papers.what_it_is: A QUBO sparse-coding formulation of single image super-resolution solved on a D-Wave Advantage quantum annealer and compared with classical annealing and Lasso.

assertions.value: The authors report that on a cropped Lenna region, quantum annealing reached a PSNR of 30.19 with an inference time of 89.60s, against 30.20 and 658.36s for classical annealing.
quotes: Result of the Classical Annealing approach showing PSNR value of 30.20 with an inference time of 658.36s. Right: Result of our Quantum Annealing approach, showing similar PSNR accuracy of 30.19 with an inference time of 89.60s.
assertions.certainty_reason: One image region on one D-Wave device.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum annealing achieves speed up over classical annealing but is far from matching Lasso Regression, and that the algorithm is distant from the deep learning-based state of the art.
quotes: while Quantum Annealing achieves speed up over Classical Annealing, it is far from matching Lasso Regression
While the proposed algorithm is distant from the deep learning-based state-of-the-art image super-resolution result
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result with the authors' own comparison.

assertions.value: The authors state that, because of limited availability of quantum computing resources for academic research, it is difficult to fully demonstrate and document the true potential of quantum computing on inference time and accuracy.
quotes: Due to the limited availability of quantum computing resources for academic research, it is difficult to fully demonstrate and document the true potential of quantum computing on the inference time and accuracy.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own stated limit, footnote 1, p.1.
